Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: 2022 Appalachian floods: 'Between July 26 and August 1, 2022, widespread and catastrophic flooding swept through portions of eastern Kentucky, southwestern Virginia, and southern West Virginia. Entire homes and parts of some communities were swept away by flood waters, leading to costly damage to infrastructure in the region.'
July 26: 'In Mingo County, the Gilbert Creek area along the Kentucky/Virginia/West Virginia border had several homes impacted and several bridges washed out, limiting access to some areas.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: nearly all buildings in the downtown area; extensive damage to the Appalachian Artisan Center, new swimming pool and skatepark; many homes and businesses heavily damaged or destroyed
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: July 28–29: 'In Hindman in Knott County, nearly all buildings in the downtown area sustained some level of flood damage from Troublesome Creek. The Appalachian Artisan Center sustained extensive damage to the museum and several studios, a new swimming pool and skatepark in town were severely damaged, and many homes and businesses were heavily damaged or destroyed.'
July 28–29: 'Upstream from Hindman, Alice Lloyd College in Pippa Passes sustained major damage due to Troublesome Creek, along with the surrounding community.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: many businesses destroyed, including a used car dealership
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: July 28–29: 'In Letcher County, Whitesburg, and surrounding communities were severely impacted by the North Fork River and Rockhouse Creek. Many businesses were destroyed in Whitesburg, including a used car dealership that had been in business for four decades.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: numerous homes and Buckhorn School completely flooded; classrooms destroyed
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: July 28–29: 'Buckhorn in Perry County was inundated by Squabble Creek, with numerous homes and Buckhorn School being completely flooded. The pavement was pulled up from the parking lot, and classrooms within the school building were destroyed ahead of the school's scheduled start date of August 11.'
July 28–29: 'Robinson Elementary in the Ary community of northern Perry County sustained exterior wall and roof collapse along Troublesome Creek, downstream of Hindman and Knott County.'
July 28–29: 'The community of Lost Creek in Breathitt County was inundated, with roads covered and homes swept off their foundations.'

July 28–29: 'The Oneida community in Clay County was cut off by downed power lines and washed-out roads and bridges, with floodwater impacting many homes that had previously been flooded by an event in March 2020.'
July 26: 'Parts of Floyd and Johnson counties were impacted by severe thunderstorms and flooding first on July 26, affecting homes and roads.'
July 28: 'More severe flooding occurred on July 28, with the towns of Martin, Wayland, and Garrett in Floyd County being among those impacted.'
July 28–29: 'In the Virgie area, south of Pikeville, Shelby Creek overran its banks and inundated several homes, leading to the closure of KY 610 in the area.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: Multiple homes (with large roof damage and one unroofed), school buildings with roof damage, concession stand and football field grandstands damaged, numerous apartment buildings, businesses, warehouses, and restaurants with significant roof and siding damage
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Table row (EF2, Owensville to western Annapolis): 'This damaging tornado first touched down in Owensville before moving north-northeastward, downing trees and tree branches. As it entered the south side of Edgewater, it strengthened and struck a subdivision, where multiple homes had large sections of their roofs torn off, and one was unroofed entirely. The Center of Applied Technology South and South River High School both sustained roof damage, while the concession stand and football field grandstands were also damaged. Many homes suffered considerable roof, siding, and porch damage as the tornado moved farther north-northeast through residential areas. After crossing the South River, the tornado reached peak strength and struck several neighborhoods in Annapolis. Numerous homes, apartment buildings, businesses, warehouses, and restaurants had their roofs ripped off or sustained significant roof and siding damage, including a warehouse that sustained some collapse of exterior walls.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: A home lost an exterior wall; another home lost a large part of its roof and siding; several other homes damaged; an outbuilding damaged; RV flipped at a business; metal storage building, turkey pens, and outbuildings damaged

A home lost an exterior wall, another home lost a large part of its roof and much of its siding, and several other homes were damaged to a lesser degree. An outbuilding was damaged and an RV was flipped at a business near the subdivision as well. The tornado weakened as it continued to the north, damaging a metal storage building, turkey pens, outbuildings, power poles, trees, and crops before dissipating.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: Minor damage to homes in Fort Washington State Park; numerous homes with roof and siding damage in Fort Washington; in Upper Dublin: numerous homes and apartment buildings with roof loss and wall collapse; high school roof damage; large adjacent building roof loss; severe roof damage on Temple University Ambler campus; additional homes with torn roofing; minor damage to homes, commercial buildings, and a veterinary hospital
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Table row (EF2, Fort WashingtontoHorsham): '1 death – This rain-wrapped, strong tornado touched down near the Philadelphia Cricket Clubsouthwest ofWhitemarsh, where minor low-end EF1 tree damage occurred. Additional minor damage occurred to homes and trees in and around Fort Washington State Park. The tornado strengthened to high-end EF1 intensity as it moved through Whitemarsh, crossed the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and moved into a more residential area as it entered Fort Washington, where many trees were snapped, and numerous homes sustained minor to moderate roof and siding damage. The tornado then rapidly intensified and reached its peak intensity of high-end EF2 as it crossed PA 309 in Upper Dublin. Numerous homes and apartment buildings sustained partial to total loss of their roofs, and one sustained collapse of some exterior walls. Upper Dublin High Schoolsustained roof damage, a large building adjacent to the school lost a significant portion of its roof, and power poles were snapped. Homes near the school were damaged, and one woman was killed when a large tree fell onto her house on Kenyon Drive. The tornado weakened to high-end EF1 strength as it continued to move to the northeast, flattening a wide swath of trees in a wooded area and causing severe roof damage to buildings on the campus of Temple University Ambler. Homes were damaged in a nearby neighborhood as well, a few of which also had large sections of roofing torn off. Many additional trees were downed, and mostly minor roof damage to homes, commercial buildings, and a veterinary hospital occurred in Maple Glen before the tornado quickly dissipated.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: A few homes sustained minor damage
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Table row (EF1, Edgewater Park, NJtoBristol, PA): 'This tornado came from the same storm that produced the Mullica Hill EF3 tornado. Trees and power lines were damaged along the path and a few homes sustained minor damage.'
Table row (EF0, Dennis): 'A weak tornado caused minor damage to two homes in town, and knocked down three large oak trees.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: Multiple homes with significant structural damage; one home nearly destroyed; commercial farm barns and storage buildings destroyed; several two‐story homes with total roof and wall loss; one house completely leveled; barns and silos destroyed at a dairy farm; additional homes with roof damage in Mantua Township; large commercial greenhouse partially destroyed; garages destroyed and a fire station damaged in Wenonah; minor damage in Woodbury Heights and Deptford
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Cedar Grove–Mullica Hill–Wenonah–Deptford, New Jersey section: 'This intense wedge tornado caused major damage as it paralleled Route 45 to its west in Gloucester County. It first touched down at 6:10 p.m. EDT (22:10 UTC), east-southeast of Harrisonville, initially causing minor tree damage. Tree damage became more significant as it moved northeast into the eastern side of Cedar Grove, and dozens of trees were downed at EF1 intensity in the small community. The tornado became strong and destructive as it struck the Willow Oaks subdivision at the northeast edge of Cedar Grove, where multiple homes sustained significant structural damage on Marvin Lane. Roofs were ripped off, exterior walls were collapsed, vehicles were moved and damaged, and one home was left with only a few walls left standing, with the damage in this area being rated EF3. The tornado then weakened momentarily as it struck a commercial farm along Route 77 at the south edge of Mullica Hill, destroying barns and storage buildings at EF1 to EF2 intensity before strengthening again and moving through a subdivision in the eastern part of town. The large tornado reached its peak intensity of mid-range EF3 at this location as it moved over Salvatore Lane and Clems Run. Several two‐story homes sustained total roof and exterior wall loss in this area, and cars were tossed around. One house was completely leveled, though it was not well-anchored and nearby trees did not sustain damage consistent with a tornado stronger than EF3 strength. Crossing US 322 past Mullica Hill, the tornado maintained its strength as it destroyed barns and silos at a large dairy farm, and completely mowed down a wide swath of large trees as it moved through a wooded area. In the worst affected area, every tree in the direct path was snapped near the base. The tornado then briefly weakened to EF1 intensity before regaining EF2 intensity as it moved into Mantua Township and passed west of Barnsboro, where many trees were downed, homes sustained roof damage, and a large commercial greenhouse was partially destroyed. Continuing to the northeast, it remained at EF2 strength as it impacted Wenonah, where garages were destroyed, a fire station was damaged, and some homes had roofs and exterior walls ripped off. The tornado then narrowed and gradually weakened, causing mostly minor damage to trees, fences, roofs and siding in Woodbury Heights and Deptford before dissipating at 6:30 p.m. EDT (22:30 UTC).'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Damage header: Large parts of northern England and Scotland lost access to electricity. 50,000 households were without electricity for more than 24 hours, with some supplies not restored until the New Year. Six electricity companies in Great Britain declared a systems emergency as a result of the damage. The reactors at Hunterston B nuclear power station were shut down when power was lost, possibly due to arcing at pylons caused by salt spray from the sea. When the grid connection was restored, the generators that had powered the station during the blackout were shut down and left on 'manual start', so when the power failed again the station was powered by batteries for a short time of around 30 minutes, until the diesel generators were started manually. During this period the reactors were left without forced cooling, in a similar fashion to the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster, but the event at Hunterston was rated as INES 2.

Total_Summary_Affected.Total_Affected_Annotation: 1972 Hong Kong landslides header: 'A series of major landslides occurred in Hong Kong in June 1972. Several apartment complexes and houses were wiped out, and at least 156 people lost their lives.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Shiu Fai Terrace header: 'Multiple landslides also occurred at Shiu Fai Terrace in Wan Chai. In total, three large landslips occurred over a continuous area on June 16. They were not as large as the Po Shan Road disaster but altogether affected a greater area. Several were killed by the landslips. Throughout June 1972, multiple incidents of landslides occurred throughout Hong Kong, especially in Wan Chai. In total, combined with the Po Shan and Shiu Fai landslides, the landslips killed around 148 people.'

Sau Mau Ping landslide header: 'At midday on 18 June, a landslide buried a squatter village at the Sau Mau Ping licensed area, killing 71. The mud spilled over Tsui Ping Road into the Kwun Tong Resettlement Estate. Resettlement Department staff and fathers of the adjacent Kwun Tong Maryknoll College launched the rescue operation. They were joined by 600 personnel from the army, police, fire services, Civil Aid Service, and Auxiliary Medical Service. Many of those killed were children. Survivors were billeted at the Kun Tong Police Station and the Sau Mau Ping Resettlement Estate. The collapsed hill slope was reconstructed with a gentler grade. The disaster site is now home to the Sau Mau Ping Memorial Park, opened 1976.'

Po Shan Road landslide header: 'On June 16, 1972, several minor slips of mud were noticed along Po Shan Road. On June 17, a slip occurred at the southern face of Inland Lot 2260, and on June 18, as the situation worsened with continuous rain, a huge mass broke free—first breaking through a retaining wall on Kotewall Road and later, after 8 p.m., an even larger landslip cleared a path from Po Shan Road to Kotewall Road, destroying houses and causing severe damage. This final slip resulted in 67 people being killed and 20 injured in less than a minute.'

Additionally, the playing field, ground level facilities (such as locker rooms), and service entrance of LP Field were under water.
Nashville and Davidson County: The basement flooded in Schermerhorn Symphony Center, causing the destruction of two Steinway grand concert pianos and one organ valued at $2.5 million.
Nashville and Davidson County: The common areas of the Gaylord Opryland Hotel were destroyed, with parts of the hotel submerged under 10 feet of water at the flood's peak.
Nashville and Davidson County: WSM's administrative offices next to the Grand Ole Opry House were completely destroyed and later demolished.
Nashville and Davidson County: Neighboring Opry Mills mall was inundated and remained closed until March 29, 2012.
Nashville and Davidson County: Flooding was reported in a mechanical room of the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum, although the exhibits were not damaged.

Nashville and Davidson County: 40 feet (12 m) of water filled the underground parking garage of The Pinnacle at Symphony Place, damaging electric and elevator systems in this 417‐foot tower in downtown.
Nashville and Davidson County: In Belle Meade, a neighborhood of Nashville, the ground floor of St. George's Episcopal Church was flooded.
Nashville and Davidson County: The newsroom of WTVF was flooded and remained nonoperational for 3 months.
Nashville and Davidson County: The Harrington water treatment plant, one of two in the city, flooded, prompting water use restrictions on May 3.

Nashville and Davidson County: The Dry Creek wastewater treatment plant in Madison was flooded, with some equipment areas submerged under more than 40 feet of water, requiring about a month for full process recovery.
Hickman County: The Duck River at Centerville exceeded its record level by nearly 10 feet, flooding or destroying homes, roads, and agricultural land.
Montgomery County: The Cumberland River in Clarksville flooded many businesses along the river, leading to closures of these establishments for up to seven weeks.
Montgomery County: All schools in the Clarksville-Montgomery County School System were closed for at least two weeks due to flooding.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Avalon–Cascilla–Otoucalofa–Tula, Mississippi: This long‐tracked tornado family caused at least 19 deaths in Leflore County as it leveled many small homes. Three of the fatalities occurred near Itta Bena and Greenwood. In Carroll County, the tornado caused five additional deaths near Avalon. The tornado also impacted and hurled a school bus for 50 yd (46 m); 11 children and the driver sustained injuries. As it traversed Grenada County, the tornado struck another school bus and killed a child. Nearby, the tornado obliterated a house and claimed three more lives. Three other people died in another home near Cascilla in Tallahatchie County. The tornado generated its worst damage in Otoucalofa, known then as O'Tuckalofa, near Water Valley — killing 19 people — and northwest of Tula, five more deaths occurred. In all, the tornado injured 500 people and caused $600,000 in losses.

Barrville–Lacon, Illinois: This violent tornado touched down east of Kickapoo and impacted areas near Alta and on the northwestern outskirts of Chillicothe before striking Barrville. Near the river, it caused one fatality. As it entered Lacon, the tornado destroyed a quarter of the town – three deaths occurred there. About 3 mi farther on, it produced F5-level damage to a farmhouse and killed three people. Along its entire path, about 70 injuries were reported.
